objectives.label: Equal ordered pairs
objectives.description: Find unknown values by equating the corresponding components of equal ordered pairs, and plot ordered pairs.

objectives.label: Finding cartesian products
objectives.description: Find the cartesian product X×Y of two finite sets, including X², and calculate the number of its elements n(X×Y).

objectives.label: Arrow and cartesian diagrams
objectives.description: Represent the cartesian product of finite sets by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Graphing infinite cartesian products
objectives.description: Represent products of infinite sets such as N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q and R×R on a perpendicular graphical net, identify ordered pairs of points, and locate points by quadrant or axis.

passages.text: Are the number of elements of $X\times Y$ = the number of elements of $Y\times X$?

A.why: It asks the student to compare the number of elements of X×Y and Y×X, which is work to be done, not a framing of why or what.

B.why: A question asking the student to work out whether n(X×Y) equals n(Y×X), not a look back.

passages.text: In this case, X × X can be represented graphically by 9 points where each point represents an ordered pair. But if X is an infinite set then the number of elements of X×X is infinite.

A.why: It says X×X can be shown as points, each an ordered pair, and is infinite when X is infinite, which leads into graphing products.

B.why: It explains that X×X for an infinite set has infinitely many elements, leading to graphs of infinite products.

passages.text: How can you represent the cartesian product of each of the following? N × N, Z × Z, Q × Q and R × R.

A.why: It asks how to represent N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q and R×R, which sets up graphing infinite products.

B.why: It asks how to represent N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q and R×R graphically, introducing the idea of graphing infinite products.

passages.text: For Example: point A represents the ordered pair (3, 2) and point B represents (0, 4).

A.why: It is an example of points A and B read as ordered pairs.

B.why: An example of reading points A and B as ordered pairs.

passages.text: We represent the set of integers on each of the two horizontal and vertical straight lines where the point (O) represents the ordered pair (0, 0).

A.why: It is a step in building the graphical net, placing integers on the lines with O as (0, 0).

B.why: A step in setting up the graphical net with integers on the axes.

passages.text: The set of real numbers can be represented on each of the two horizontal and vertical straight lines, and point O represents the ordered pair (o, o).

A.why: It is a step in building the net for the real numbers, with O as (0, 0).

B.why: A statement of how real numbers sit on the axes and where O is, with no motivating idea.

passages.text: Then, the net is divided into four parts (quadrants) as in the opposite figure.

A.why: It is a side note that the net is divided into four quadrants, with no motivation given.

B.why: A description of how the net is divided into quadrants, not a motivating situation or a reflection.

objectives.label: Write relations as ordered pairs
objectives.description: Write a relation from a set X to a set Y as a set of ordered pairs, using the rule connecting a and b (e.g. b = 2a + 4, or 'a is a digit of b').

objectives.label: Represent relations by diagrams
objectives.description: Represent a relation by an arrow diagram and by a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Relations as subsets of X × Y
objectives.description: Determine whether a relation is a subset of the cartesian product X × Y, decide which ordered pairs satisfy the stated relation, and identify a relation on a set X as R ⊂ X × X.

passages.text: Is R a subset from the cartesian product $X \times Z$?

A.why: It asks the student to work out whether R is a subset of X × Z, so it is a question to solve and not an introduction or a reflection.

B.why: It asks the student to decide whether R is a subset of X × Z, which is work to do, not an introduction or a reflection.

objectives.label: Identify functions
objectives.description: Decide whether a relation, given as arrow diagram, cartesian diagram or ordered pairs, is a function by checking that each element of X has only one image.

objectives.label: Symbolic representation of functions
objectives.description: Write a function using the symbols f : X \to Y, f(x) = y and as a set of ordered pairs, and represent it by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Domain, codomain and range
objectives.description: Determine the domain, codomain and range of a function, noting the range is a subset of the codomain.

passages.text: The following figures represent three relations from X to Y.

A.why: It only points to the figures showing three relations, so it is a setup line with no idea or situation.

B.why: It only points to figures of three relations from X to Y; it is an instruction-like lead-in with no real situation or idea.

passages.text: Is every relation a function? Explain your answer and give examples.

A.why: It asks whether every relation is a function, which opens the idea of what makes a relation a function.

B.why: It asks the student to work out and justify whether every relation is a function, so it is neither an intro nor a closing reflection.

passages.text: If f is a function from X to Y, i.e. $f: X \to Y$, then

A.why: It starts a formal statement of the notation f: X → Y, so it is a definition and not a motivating idea.

B.why: It starts a definition/notation statement for f: X → Y, not a motivating situation or a reflection.

objectives.label: Identify polynomials and degree
objectives.description: Identify polynomial functions and state their degree from the function rule.

objectives.label: Evaluate function values
objectives.description: Calculate the image of a given value (including surds) under a polynomial function.

objectives.label: Graph linear and constant functions
objectives.description: Represent a linear function or constant function graphically by finding ordered pairs and drawing the straight line.

objectives.label: Graph quadratic functions
objectives.description: Represent a quadratic function graphically and state its vertex, axis of symmetry and maximum or minimum value.

passages.text: For example: f(x) = 3 and it is written as y = 3

A.why: It is an example of a constant function, f(x) = 3, not an introduction.

B.why: It is an example of a constant function, f(x) = 3, written as y = 3.

passages.text: It is represented by a straight line paralled to the x-axis.

A.why: It is a side note on how the graph of a constant function looks, with no situation or reflection.

B.why: It is a side note describing how the graph looks, not a motivating situation or reflection.

A.why: It introduces what a quadratic function f(x) = ax² + bx + c is and its properties, with no worked numbers.

B.why: It restates the general quadratic form and leads into a list of properties, with no outside situation or why-idea.
